# ECON 0100 | Exercise E3 | Monopoly

::: solution

# Solutions

:::

## Warmup | One Price for Everyone

You sell 20 units at \$100 each. To sell 30 units, you must lower the price to \$90 on every unit.

a\) What is total revenue at 20 units? At 30 units?\
b\) How much additional revenue do the 10 extra units bring in, on average, per unit?\
c\) Why is your answer to b less than \$90?

::: solution

**a)** Revenue is **2,000** at 20 units and **2,700** at 30 units: $100 \times 20$ and $90 \times 30$.

**b)** **70 per additional unit, on average:** $(2700 - 2000)/(30 - 20) = 70$.

**c)** The 10 extra units bring in 900, but lowering the price on the original 20 units loses $20 \times 10 = 200$. Net additional revenue is $900 - 200 = 700$.

:::

## Q1 | Marginal Revenue

Demand is $P = 120 - Q$, and the firm charges the same price for every unit.

a\) Find the price and total revenue at $Q = 40$ and at $Q = 50$.

b\) Calculate the change in total revenue, then marginal revenue averaged over these 10 additional units.

::: solution

**a)** At $Q = 40$: **price 80; total revenue 3,200**. At $Q = 50$: **price 70; total revenue 3,500**.

**b)** **Additional revenue 300; average marginal revenue 30:** $(3500 - 3200)/(50 - 40) = 30$. This is the average across the interval; $MR = 120 - 2Q$ falls from 40 to 20 between its endpoints.

:::

\newpage

## Q2 | Choosing Quantity, Price, and Profit

Suppose demand rises to $P = 160 - Q$, so $MR = 160 - 2Q$. The monopolist’s marginal cost is still $MC = 2Q$, with fixed cost of 1,200. Its cost curves are shown below.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

a\) Calculate and graph the profit-maximizing quantity.

b\) Calculate and graph the price that lets the firm sell that quantity.

c\) Calculate and graph the firm’s maximum profit.\
(*Hint: $ATC$ at the profit-maximizing quantity is 70.*)

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

**a)** **40 units.** Set $MR = MC$: $160 - 2Q = 2Q$, so $Q = 40$.

**b)** **Price 120.** Use demand: $P = 160 - 40 = 120$. The MR–MC intersection gives quantity; demand gives the price buyers will pay for that quantity.

**c)** **Profit 2,000:** $(120 - 70) \times 40 = 2000$. The vertical bars between price and ATC, from zero to 40 units, show profit. The cost curve is $ATC = Q + 1200/Q$, giving $ATC(40) = 70$.

:::

\newpage

## Q3 | The Missing Trades

Return to the original demand: $P = 120 - Q$, with $MR = 120 - 2Q$ and $MC = 2Q$. The monopolist chooses $Q = 30$ and $P = 90$. There are no externalities.

:::: {.columns gutter=1em}

::: {.column width=60%}

a\) At $Q = 30$, buyers’ willingness to pay is 90 and marginal cost is 60. Why does the monopolist stop here instead of producing where $P = MC$?

b\) Calculate and mark the socially efficient quantity.

c\) Calculate and shade the deadweight loss from monopoly.

:::

::: {.column width=40%}

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,){width=100%}

:::

::::

::: solution

**a)** Selling more requires cutting the price on every unit. The monopolist compares **MR with MC**: at $Q = 30$, both equal 60. Beyond 30, MR falls below MC, so profit falls even though buyers’ willingness to pay still exceeds the resource cost. For a whole extra unit, revenue rises by 59 while cost rises by 61.

**b)** **40 units.** With no externalities, demand is marginal benefit. Set $P = MC$: $120 - Q = 2Q$, so $Q = 40$.

**c)** **Deadweight loss is 150:** $\frac{1}{2} \times (40 - 30) \times (90 - 60) = 150$. The vertical bars between demand and MC from 30 to 40 represent gains from trades the monopolist does not make. This lost surplus is distinct from the firm’s profit.

:::
